cards.title: 2.1.1 Temperature and the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
body: **Thermodynamics** is the area of physics concerned with the relationship between heat and work.
The laws of thermodynamics describe what happens as energy is transformed into work or work is transformed into energy.
**Temperature** is the degree of hotness or coldness of an object.
The temperature of an object is a measure of how hot or cold the object is.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Temperature Scales
body: **A thermometer** is a device that measures temperature.
The operation of a thermometer depends on some physical property that changes continuously and regularly with change of temperature.
The thermometric property (temperature dependent property) most commonly used to measure temperature is thermal expansion.
Nearly all substances expand with increasing temperature and contract with decreasing temperature.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Thermometers
body: **Thermometry** is the science of temperature measurement.
Any material solid, liquid, or gas that expands uniformly over a certain temperature range can be used in a thermometer.
**The thermometer** is an instrument used for measuring the temperature of a body.
The operation of a thermometer is based on a measurable physical change which goes with a temperature change.

cards.title: 2.1.4 Heat and its Units
body: If a small amount of hot water is poured into a cup of cold water the water in the cup becomes warmer.
The temperature of an object will rise if the average kinetic energy of its molecules is increased.
Internal energy includes the kinetic, potential, chemical, nuclear, electrical energy and all other forms of energy possessed by the molecules of an object.
James Prescott Joule (1818–1889) showed that heat is related to energy.

cards.title: 2.1.6 Latent Heat
body: When water at room temperature is heated, the temperature rises steadily until it reaches its boiling point (100 qC).
The heat that produces a change in temperature of a substance without a change in state is called a **sensible heat**.
When the temperature reaches 100 qC the water continues to receive heat energy, but the temperature remains constant.
At this temperature, the heat added starts to change the state of water from liquid to steam or vapour.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: If the temperature of a substance increases by $$15^\circ\text{C}$$, what is the corresponding increase on the Kelvin scale?

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand temperature changes versus absolute temperatures**
An absolute temperature conversion is given by $$T_K = T_C + 273.15$$.
**Step 2: Analyze temperature intervals (differences)**
Since the Celsius and Kelvin degrees are identical in size, any temperature change ($\Delta T$) is identical on both scales:
$$\Delta T_K = \Delta T_C$$
**Step 3: Apply the given values**
$$\Delta T_C = 15^\circ\text{C} \implies \Delta T_K = 15\text{ K}$$
**Step 4: Final Result**
The temperature increase on the Kelvin scale is **$$15\text{ K}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why does water have a major regulatory effect on global climates and coastal temperatures?

options.A: It has an extremely low specific heat capacity.
options.B: It has an exceptionally high specific heat capacity.
options.C: It is a highly efficient thermal conductor.
options.D: It undergoes sublimation easily at room temperature.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand specific heat capacity physical meaning**
Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat required to change the temperature of $$1\text{ kg}$$ of a substance by $$1\text{ K}$$.

**Step 2: Connect to water properties**
Water has a very high specific heat capacity ($$c \approx 4200\text{ J/kgK}$$). This means it can absorb or release vast amounts of thermal energy with minimal changes in its own temperature.

**Step 3: Connect to climate behavior**
This thermal stability allows oceans to act as heat reservoirs, preventing extreme temperature swings in coastal regions.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The correct option is **It has an exceptionally high specific heat capacity.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following processes describes heat transfer through a vacuum without requiring any physical medium?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze heat transfer mechanisms**
- **Conduction** requires atomic/molecular collisions (solid medium).
- **Convection** requires bulk movement of fluid masses (liquid/gas medium).
- **Radiation** transfers heat via electromagnetic waves.

**Step 2: Determine vacuum propagation capabilities**
Electromagnetic waves do not require any physical medium and propagate through a vacuum at the speed of light.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct process is **Radiation**.

cards.title: 2.1 Temperature and Heat
body: **Temperature** is a quantitative measure of the average kinetic energy of the atoms or molecules in a substance, while **heat** is the spontaneous transfer of thermal energy between systems due to a temperature gradient.

cards.title: 2.1 Temperature and Heat — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: To understand thermodynamics, we must distinguish between temperature and heat. Temperature is an intensive property, meaning it does not depend on the quantity of matter. It dictates the direction of spontaneous heat flow: thermal energy always flows from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. This concept is formalized by the **Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics**, which states that if two thermodynamic systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This law justifies the use of thermometers as objective measuring devices.

Historically, various temperature scales were devised based on different reference physical states of water. The **Celsius scale** assigns $$0^\circ\text{C}$$ to the freezing point and $$100^\circ\text{C}$$ to the boiling point of pure water under standard atmospheric pressure. The **Fahrenheit scale** sets these points at $$32^\circ\text{F}$$ and $$212^\circ\text{F}$$, resulting in a fundamental interval of $$180$$ divisions instead of the Celsius scale's $$100$$. The conversions are governed by the linear equation: $$T_F = \frac{9}{5}T_C + 32$$.

The **Kelvin scale**, also known as the absolute temperature scale, has its zero point ($$0\text{ K}$$) at **absolute zero**, the theoretical state where all classical molecular motion ceases. Because a Kelvin degree is identical in size to a Celsius degree, the conversion is: $$T_K = T_C + 273.15$$. Absolute zero corresponds to $$-273.15^\circ\text{C}$$. On the Kelvin scale, temperatures can never be negative.

When thermal energy (heat) is added to a system without changing its state, its temperature rises. The quantity of heat ($$Q$$) required is proportional to the mass ($$m$$) and the temperature change ($$\Delta T$$). The constant of proportionality is the **specific heat capacity** ($$c$$), defined by the equation: $$Q = mc\Delta T$$. Water has an exceptionally high specific heat capacity ($$c \approx 4200\text{ J}/(\text{kg}\cdot\text{K})$$), which enables oceans to regulate global climates.

cards.title: 2.1 Temperature and Heat — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: During a phase transition (such as melting ice or boiling water), heat is absorbed or released without any change in temperature. This thermal energy is used to break intermolecular bonds rather than increase molecular kinetic energy. The heat required per unit mass for a phase change is called **latent heat** ($$L$$), expressed as: $$Q = mL$$. The latent heat of fusion ($$L_f$$) applies to solid-to-liquid transitions, while the latent heat of vaporization ($$L_v$$) applies to liquid-to-gas transitions.

cards.title: 2.1 Temperature and Heat — Comparison of Temperature Scales
body: Temperature Reference Point — Celsius Scale ($$^\circ\text{C}$$) — Fahrenheit Scale ($$^\circ\text{F}$$) — Kelvin Scale (\text{K}) | Absolute Zero — $$-273.15$$ — $$-459.67$$ — $$0$$ | Freezing Point of Water — $$0$$ — $$32$$ — $$273.15$$ | Boiling Point of Water — $$100$$ — $$212$$ — $$373.15$$

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Absolute zero ($$0\text{ K}$$) is a theoretical limit. While scientists have cooled substances to within a billionth of a degree of absolute zero, the Third Law of Thermodynamics dictates that it is physically impossible to reach absolute zero in a finite number of steps.

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When solving calorimetry problems, the total heat lost by the warmer substances must equal the total heat gained by the cooler substances: $$Q_{\text{lost}} = Q_{\text{gained}}$$. Always write this conservation of energy equation first.

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the nature of heat**
Heat is a transfer of thermal energy between systems.

**Step 2: Recall the SI unit of energy**
Since heat is a form of energy in transit, its standard SI unit must be the same as the unit for energy and work.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The SI unit of heat is the **Joule**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which medium is heat transfer by convection primarily restricted to?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define convection**
Convection is heat transfer by macroscopic movement of bulk portions of a material due to density variations.

**Step 2: Identify medium requirements**
For mass movement to occur, the molecules must be free to migrate over long distances. This behavior is physically restricted to fluids (liquids and gases).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Convection is restricted to **Fluids (liquids and gases)**.

cards.title: 2.2 Transfer of Heat
body: **Heat Transfer** is the movement of thermal energy from a system of higher temperature to a system of lower temperature through three physical mechanisms: conduction, convection, and radiation.

cards.title: 2.2 Transfer of Heat — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: Conduction is the process of heat transfer through a material medium by molecular collisions and the migration of free electrons. In solids, atoms vibrate about their fixed lattice positions; when heated, these vibrations become more energetic and are transmitted to neighboring atoms. Metals are highly efficient thermal conductors because they contain a sea of highly mobile free electrons that quickly transfer kinetic energy throughout the material. The rate of heat flow by conduction ($$\frac{Q}{t}$$) through a slab of material is given by Fourier's Law: $$\frac{Q}{t} = \frac{kA\Delta T}{L}$$, where $$k$$ is the thermal conductivity of the material, $$A$$ is the cross-sectional area, $$\Delta T$$ is the temperature difference across the material, and $$L$$ is the thickness.

Convection is the transfer of heat within fluid media (liquids and gases) via the physical movement of the fluid itself. When a fluid is heated from below, it expands, becomes less dense, and rises due to buoyant forces. The cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place, establishing a **convection current**. Natural convection drives global wind patterns, ocean currents, and tectonic plate movements. Forced convection occurs when a fan or pump actively circulates the heated fluid, as seen in car radiators and cooling fans for computer processors.

Radiation is the transfer of thermal energy via electromagnetic waves (primarily infrared radiation). Unlike conduction and convection, radiation does not require any material medium; it can propagate through a vacuum at the speed of light. Every object with a temperature above absolute zero continuously emits electromagnetic radiation. The rate of energy emission is governed by the Stefan-Boltzmann Law: $$P = \sigma e A T^4$$, where $$\sigma$$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $$e$$ is the emissivity of the surface, $$A$$ is the surface area, and $$T$$ is the absolute temperature in Kelvin.

cards.title: 2.2 Transfer of Heat — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: Why it matters: Understanding heat transfer is essential for building insulation, manufacturing energy-efficient windows, and designing spacesuits that protect astronauts from extreme solar radiation and absolute cold. It also explains how double-walled thermos flasks work: the vacuum between the double walls eliminates conduction and convection, while the silvered inner surfaces minimize radiation losses.

cards.title: 2.2 Transfer of Heat — Comparison of Heat Transfer Mechanisms
body: Mechanism — Medium Requirement — Physical Mechanism — Governing Scientific Law | Conduction — Required (primarily solids) — Molecular vibrations and free electron movement — Fourier's Law of Conduction | Convection — Required (fluids only) — Macroscopic mass movement of fluid densities — Newton's Law of Cooling | Radiation — Not Required (vacuum or transparent media) — Electromagnetic waves (infrared) — Stefan-Boltzmann Law

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The Earth is warmed by the Sun entirely through radiation. Because the vast space between the Sun and the Earth is a near-perfect vacuum, conduction and convection cannot transfer any energy to us.

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: Air is an exceptionally poor conductor of heat. Double-pane windows and thermal blankets exploit this by trapping pockets of still air, which drastically reduces heat loss via conduction and prevents the setup of convection currents.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Heat reaches the Earth from the Sun mainly by:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Conduction and convection need a material medium (particles).

**Step 2:** Space between the Sun and the Earth is almost a vacuum.

**Step 3:** Answer: only radiation (electromagnetic waves) can cross a vacuum.

**Tip:** Conduction – solids; convection – liquids and gases; radiation – no medium needed.

cards.title: Formula
body: ΔU = Q − W
First law (school sign: W work done by the system). Heat in raises U or does work or both.

cards.title: 2.3.1 The First Law of Thermodynamics
body: Everything that is not part of the system is considered to be external to the system or, in other words, is the surroundings of the system.
A closed system is one in which no mass enters or leaves.
A closed system is said to be isolated if no energy in any form passes across its boundaries.
If no heat enters or leaves the system during some process, then the system is said to be isolated from its environment.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Thermodynamic Processes
body: All of these properties are state variables.
**A state variable** is a physical property that characterizes the state of a system independently of how that particular state is reached.
**A thermodynamic process** is the method by which a system is changed from one state to another.
The state of a system is described by a set of state variables such as pressure, temperature, volume, mass and internal energy.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: According to the sign conventions of the First Law of Thermodynamics ($$\Delta U = Q - W$$), how are the signs of $$Q$$ and $$W$$ defined when heat is added to the system and work is done ON the system?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall First Law sign conventions**
- Heat ($$Q$$): Heat entering (added to) the system is positive ($$Q > 0$$). Heat leaving is negative ($$Q < 0$$).
- Work ($$W$$): Work done BY the system (expansion) is positive ($$W > 0$$). Work done ON the system (compression) is negative ($$W < 0$$).

**Step 2: Apply the given conditions**
- Heat is added to the system: $$Q > 0$$
- Work is done ON the system: $$W < 0$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct sign combination is **$$Q > 0$$ and $$W < 0$$**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: According to the sign conventions of the First Law of Thermodynamics ($$\Delta U = Q - W$$), how are the signs of $$Q$$ and $$W$$ defined when heat is added to the system and work is done ON the system?

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall First Law sign conventions**
- Heat ($$Q$$): Heat entering (added to) the system is positive ($$Q > 0$$). Heat leaving is negative ($$Q < 0$$).
- Work ($$W$$): Work done BY the system (expansion) is positive ($$W > 0$$). Work done ON the system (compression) is negative ($$W < 0$$).
**Step 2: Apply the given conditions**
- Heat is added to the system: $$Q > 0$$
- Work is done ON the system: $$W < 0$$
**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct sign combination is **$$Q > 0$$ and $$W < 0$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is always true for an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define an isothermal process**
An isothermal process is one during which the temperature of the system remains strictly constant:
$$\Delta T = 0$$

**Step 2: Apply to an ideal gas**
The internal energy ($$U$$) of an ideal gas depends solely on its absolute temperature ($$T$$). Therefore, if temperature is constant, internal energy must also be constant:
$$U = \text{constant} \implies \Delta U = 0$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
For an isothermal process of an ideal gas, **$$\Delta U = 0$$** is always true.

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: 2.3 The First Law of Thermodynamics and Thermodynamic Processes
body: The **First Law of Thermodynamics** is a manifestation of the law of conservation of energy applied to thermodynamic systems, stating that the change in internal energy ($$\Delta U$$) of a closed system is equal to the net heat ($$Q$$) added to the system minus the net work ($$W$$) done by the system.

cards.title: 2.3 The First Law of Thermodynamics and Thermodynamic Processes — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: Internal energy ($$U$$) is the sum of all microscopic kinetic and potential energies of the molecules making up a thermodynamic system. It is a state function, meaning its value depends solely on the current state of the system, not on the path taken to reach that state. On the other hand, heat ($$Q$$) and work ($$W$$) are path functions; they describe energy in transit. The First Law of Thermodynamics is mathematically written as: $$\Delta U = Q - W$$. Here, $$Q$$ is positive when heat enters the system and negative when heat leaves. $$W$$ is positive when work is done by the system on its surroundings (causing expansion) and negative when work is done on the system by the surroundings (causing compression).

When a gas is held in a cylinder with a movable piston, the work done during an infinitesimal change in volume ($$dV$$) is given by: $$dW = P dV$$. For a finite change from an initial volume $$V_i$$ to a final volume $$V_f$$ at constant pressure (an **isobaric process**), the work done is: $$W = P(V_f - V_i) = P\Delta V$$. This work corresponds to the area under the curve on a pressure-volume (**PV diagram**).

In an **isothermal process**, the temperature of the system remains constant ($$\Delta T = 0$$). For an ideal gas, the internal energy depends only on temperature, so $$\Delta U = 0$$. Consequently, the First Law reduces to: $$Q = W$$. This means that all heat added to an ideal gas during an isothermal expansion is converted entirely into mechanical work.

An **adiabatic process** occurs when no heat is transferred into or out of the system ($$Q = 0$$). This can be achieved by insulating the system or by performing the process so rapidly that heat does not have time to flow. For an adiabatic process, the First Law becomes: $$\Delta U = -W$$. If the gas expands adiabatically ($$W > 0$$), its internal energy must decrease ($$\Delta U < 0$$), causing the gas temperature to drop. Conversely, adiabatic compression increases the internal energy and temperature.

cards.title: 2.3 The First Law of Thermodynamics and Thermodynamic Processes — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: In an **isochoric (or isovolumetric) process**, the volume of the system remains constant ($$\Delta V = 0$$). Since there is no displacement, the work done is zero ($$W = 0$$). The First Law simplifies to: $$\Delta U = Q$$. Thus, any thermal energy added to the system goes entirely into increasing its internal energy and temperature.

cards.title: 2.3 The First Law of Thermodynamics and Thermodynamic Processes — Thermodynamic Processes Summary
body: Process Type — Constant Parameter — First Law Simplification — Physical Significance | Isothermal — Temperature ($$T = \text{const}$$) — $$\Delta U = 0 \implies Q = W$$ — Heat added equals work done by gas | Adiabatic — Heat flow ($$Q = 0$$) — $$\Delta U = -W$$ — Compression heats gas; expansion cools gas | Isobaric — Pressure ($$P = \text{const}$$) — $$\Delta U = Q - P\Delta V$$ — Work is represented by $$P\Delta V$$ | Isochoric — Volume ($$V = \text{const}$$) — $$\Delta U = Q \implies W = 0$$ — Heat added increases internal energy only

> **💡 Did You Know?**: When you spray an aerosol can (like spray paint or deodorant) for a long time, the can becomes very cold. This is a real-world example of an adiabatic expansion: the gas inside expands rapidly, performing work against atmospheric pressure, which forces its internal energy and temperature to drop.

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To easily remember the sign conventions of the First Law, think of a steam engine. We put heat *into* the engine ($$Q > 0$$) to get mechanical work *out* of the engine ($$W > 0$$). Both of these actions are positive.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: When an ideal gas undergoes a rapid adiabatic expansion, its temperature:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define an adiabatic expansion**
- Adiabatic: No heat transfer occurs ($$Q = 0$$).
- Expansion: Gas does work on surroundings ($$W > 0$$).

**Step 2: Apply the First Law of Thermodynamics**
$$\Delta U = Q - W$$
$$\Delta U = 0 - W = -W$$
Since $$W > 0$$, the change in internal energy is negative:
$$\Delta U < 0$$

**Step 3: Relate to temperature**
For an ideal gas, a decrease in internal energy ($$\Delta U < 0$$) directly corresponds to a decrease in temperature ($$\Delta T < 0$$).

**Step 4: Final Result**
The temperature **Decreases**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In an isochoric thermodynamic process, which of the following quantities is strictly zero?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define an isochoric process**
An isochoric (isovolumetric) process is one in which the volume of the system remains constant:
$$\Delta V = 0$$

**Step 2: Calculate work done**
Work done by a gas is given by:
$$W = \int P dV$$
Since volume is constant ($$dV = 0$$), no boundary displacement occurs, and:
$$W = 0$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the work done ($$W$$) is strictly **Zero**.

glossary.meaning: Thermodynamics is the area of physics concerned with the relationship between heat and work.
Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of an object.
Thermal equilibrium is a situation in which two objects in thermal contact with each other cease to have a net exchange of energy.
Thermometric property is a physical property that changes continuously and regularly with change of temperature.
Heat is a transfer of energy due to temperature difference.
Heat transfer is the transmission of heat energy from a system at a higher temperature to a system at a lower temperature.
Conduction is the movement of heat as a result of collisions between molecules.
Convection is the transfer of heat by the movement of the molecules from one place to another.
Convection current is the movement of liquid and gas molecules due to heat energy that forms the circulation of liquid and gas.

questions.q: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 °C? (c = 4200 J/(kg·°C))
why: Q = mcΔθ.
questions.label: 1. How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 °C? (c = 4200 J/(kg·°C))
questions.tip: Δθ is a change, so 10 °C = 10 K.

similar.q: Water has a freezing point of 20°Y and a boiling point of 160°Y in the Y temperature scale. When the Celsius temperature is 30°C, the temperature in °Y is  A) 41.  B) 62.  C) 19.  D) 80.  E) 21.

questions.q: The same 84 000 J is given to 2 kg of copper (c = 400 J/(kg·°C)). What is its temperature rise?
why: Rearrange Q = mcΔθ: Δθ = Q/(mc).
questions.label: 2. The same 84 000 J is given to 2 kg of copper (c = 400 J/(kg·°C)). What is its temperature rise?
questions.tip: Small c → big temperature change for the same heat.

similar.q: Why seas change T slowly?
similar.a: Water’s large c.

questions.q: Why do seas and lakes change temperature slowly?
questions.answer: Water has a large specific heat capacity.
why: Q = mcΔθ, so Δθ = Q/(mc).
Water's c (4200 J/(kg·°C)) is much larger than that of soil or rock.
The same heat gives a smaller temperature change, so seas warm and cool slowly.
questions.label: 3. Why do seas and lakes change temperature slowly?
questions.tip: This is why coasts have milder climates.

similar.q: A thermodynamic process in which the volume of the system does not change is  A) isobaric.  B) adiabatic.  C) isothermal.  D) isobarometric.  E) isochoric.
similar.a: E. isochoric. — Answer: E. ('Isobarometric' is not a standard term.)

questions.q: How much energy is needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C? (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg)
questions.answer: 1.67 × 10⁵ J; the temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted.
why: Changing state uses latent heat: Q = mL_f.
questions.label: 4. How much energy is needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C? (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg)
questions.tip: During a change of state, use Q = mL, not Q = mcΔθ.

similar.q:
The amount of heat energy absorbed in joules by 50 g of iron when its temperature is raised from 30 °C to 70 °C is
[specific heat capacity of iron = 460 J/(kg·°C)]  A) 700.  B) 920.  C) 460.  D) 230.  E) 350.

questions.q: What is the difference between boiling and evaporation?
questions.answer: Boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature; evaporation happens only at the surface at any temperature.
why: Boiling: bubbles of vapour form inside the liquid at the boiling point.
Evaporation: faster molecules escape from the surface below the boiling point.
Evaporation cools the liquid; boiling keeps the temperature constant while heat is supplied.
questions.label: 5. What is the difference between boiling and evaporation?
questions.tip: Sweating cools you by evaporation.

similar.q: Best everyday conductor?
similar.a: Metals (free electrons).

questions.q: Which everyday materials are the best conductors of heat, and why?
questions.answer: Metals – they have free electrons that carry energy quickly.
why: Conduction passes energy from particle to particle.
In metals, free electrons move through the lattice and transfer energy fast.
Non-metals rely only on vibrating atoms, so they conduct poorly.
questions.label: 6. Which everyday materials are the best conductors of heat, and why?
questions.tip: Good electrical conductors are usually good heat conductors.

similar.q: Vacuum flask stops which method with which bit?
similar.a: Vacuum — conduction and convection. Silver — radiation.

questions.q: In a vacuum flask, which part stops which method of heat transfer?
questions.answer: The vacuum stops conduction and convection; the silvered walls reduce radiation.
why: Conduction and convection need particles – the vacuum has none.
Shiny silvered surfaces reflect infrared radiation.
The stopper reduces convection and evaporation at the top.
questions.label: 7. In a vacuum flask, which part stops which method of heat transfer?
questions.tip: Vacuum = no particles; silver = reflects.

similar.q: Land breeze night idea?
similar.a: Land cools faster; air slides toward the warmer sea.

questions.q: Explain a land breeze at night.
questions.answer: The land cools faster than the sea, so the air over the sea is warmer and rises; cooler air from the land flows toward the sea.
why: At night, land (low c) cools faster than the sea (high c).
Air above the warmer sea is heated, becomes less dense and rises.
Cooler, denser air from over the land moves out to replace it – a land breeze.
questions.label: 8. Explain a land breeze at night.
questions.tip: Breezes blow from the cooler surface to the warmer one (sea breeze by day, land breeze by night).

similar.q: First law in words?
similar.a: Energy conserved: heat in = rise in U + work out.

questions.q: State the first law of thermodynamics in words.
questions.answer: Energy is conserved: heat supplied = increase in internal energy + work done by the system (Q = ΔU + W).
why: Heat Q given to a gas can do two things.
It can raise the internal energy ΔU (temperature) and let the gas do work W by expanding.
So Q = ΔU + W.
questions.label: 9. State the first law of thermodynamics in words.
questions.tip: It is the law of conservation of energy applied to heat.

similar.q: A heat engine undergoes a process in which it absorbs 1500 J of heat and at the same time does 600 J of work. The change in internal energy of the heat engine, in joules, is  A) 2100.  B) 1900.  C) 1100.  D) 1000.  E) 900.
similar.a: E. 900. — ΔU = 1500 − 600 = 900 J. Answer: E. (2100 J wrongly adds the work.)

questions.q: What is an isothermal process, and what does the first law give for an ideal gas?
questions.answer: The temperature stays constant, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W.
why: Isothermal means T is constant.
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on T, so ΔU = 0.
First law: Q = ΔU + W = W – all heat in becomes work done.
questions.label: 10. What is an isothermal process, and what does the first law give for an ideal gas?
questions.tip: Iso-thermal = same temperature.

similar.q: A thermodynamic process in which the pressure of the system remains constant is  A) adiabatic process.  B) isochoric process.  C) isothermal process.  D) isometric process.  E) isobaric process.
similar.a: E. isobaric process. — G10 p.96–98: isothermal – constant temperature; isobaric – constant pressure; isochoric (isometric) – constant volume; adiabatic – no heat exchange (Q = 0). Answer: E.

questions.q: What is an adiabatic process?
questions.answer: No heat enters or leaves (Q = 0), so ΔU = −W: a gas that expands cools.
why: Adiabatic means Q = 0 (fast or insulated change).
First law: 0 = ΔU + W, so ΔU = −W.
When the gas expands (W > 0), ΔU < 0 and the temperature falls.
questions.label: 11. What is an adiabatic process?
questions.tip: A bicycle pump warms when you compress quickly – adiabatic heating.

similar.q: What is the name of a thermodynamic process in which no heat is transferred?  A) Isochoric  B) Isentropic  C) Isothermal  D) Isobaric  E) Adiabatic
similar.a: E. Adiabatic — E is keyed. B is also accepted: an isentropic process is a reversible adiabatic process, so it too involves no heat transfer (the term is not in the textbook).

questions.q: What is the SI unit of temperature?
questions.answer: The kelvin (K); a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C.
why: Kelvin is the SI base unit of temperature.
Temperature differences are the same size in both: ΔT in K = Δθ in °C.
questions.label: 12. What is the SI unit of temperature?
questions.tip: No degree sign with kelvin: write 300 K.

similar.q: The heat required, in kJ, to raise the temperature of 4 kg of iron by 5 °C is [c(iron) = 460 J/kg °C]  A) 9.2.  B) 18.4.  C) 40.6.  D) 20.3.  E) 16.5.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of heat?
questions.answer: The joule (J); the calorie is an older unit.
why: Heat is energy being transferred.
All energy in SI is measured in joules.
1 calorie ≈ 4.2 J.
questions.label: 13. What is the SI unit of heat?
questions.tip: Q in Q = mcΔθ comes out in joules if c is in J/(kg·°C).

similar.q: The two liquids used in glass thermometers are mercury and alcohol. The disadvantage of using liquid-in-glass thermometer is that  A) it can be modified for specific purposes.  B) the glass is made thin so that heat to the liquid can pass easily.  C) it gives a direct reading.  D) it is suitable for very high and very low temperatures.  E) it is simple and quick to use.
similar.a: D. it is suitable for very high and very low temperatures. — Option D is the only one about the temperature range; the paper prints 'suitable', evidently a misprint of the textbook's 'unsuitable'. Answer: D.

questions.q: Why is a burn from steam at 100 °C worse than one from water at 100 °C?
questions.answer: Condensing steam gives out its latent heat of vaporisation as well as the heat from the hot water cooling.
why: Steam on skin first condenses, releasing mL_v (2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg – very large).
The condensed water at 100 °C then cools, releasing mcΔθ.
So much more energy goes into the skin.
questions.label: 14. Why is a burn from steam at 100 °C worse than one from water at 100 °C?
questions.tip: Latent heat is released when a gas condenses.

similar.q: Black kettle in sun?
similar.a: Absorbs radiation well — heats faster.

questions.q: Why does a black kettle left in the sun warm up faster than a shiny one?
questions.answer: Dull black surfaces absorb radiation well.
why: The Sun transfers energy by radiation.
Black, dull surfaces are good absorbers (and emitters); shiny surfaces reflect.
So the black kettle absorbs more energy per second and heats faster.
questions.label: 15. Why does a black kettle left in the sun warm up faster than a shiny one?
questions.tip: Good absorbers are good emitters.

similar.q: Shiny fire-blanket side faces the fire to?
similar.a: Reflect radiation.

questions.q: Shiny fire-blanket side faces the fire to?
questions.answer: Reflect radiation.
why: Reflect radiation.
questions.label: 16. Shiny fire-blanket side faces the fire to?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Mixture method idea?
similar.a: Heat lost by hot = heat gained by cold (if no loss to air).

questions.q: What is the idea behind the method of mixtures?
questions.answer: Heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body (if none is lost to the surroundings).
why: Mix a hot and a cold substance and let them reach the same final temperature.
Energy is conserved: m₁c₁(θ₁ − θ) = m₂c₂(θ − θ₂).
Solve for the unknown c or temperature.
questions.label: 17. What is the idea behind the method of mixtures?
questions.tip: Insulate the container – heat lost to the air spoils the result.

similar.q: Thermal equilibrium?
similar.a: Same T — no net heat flow.

questions.q: What is thermal equilibrium?
questions.answer: Bodies at the same temperature – no net heat flows between them.
why: Heat flows from hotter to colder bodies.
The flow continues until the temperatures are equal.
Then the net heat flow is zero: thermal equilibrium.
questions.label: 18. What is thermal equilibrium?
questions.tip: A thermometer works because it reaches thermal equilibrium with what it measures.

similar.q: Assume that objects 'a' and 'b' are placed in thermal contact and separately in thermal equilibrium with a third object 'c' that is at 70°C. The temperature of 'a' in °C is  A) greater than 70.  B) less than 70.  C) equal to 70.  D) between 50 and 70.  E) between 70 and 90.
similar.a: C. equal to 70. — So a is at 70 °C. Answer: C.

questions.q: How much work does a gas do when it expands at constant pressure?
questions.answer: W = PΔV
why: The gas pushes a piston of area A with force F = PA.
The piston moves a distance d, so W = Fd = PAd.
Ad = ΔV, so W = PΔV.
questions.label: 19. How much work does a gas do when it expands at constant pressure?
questions.tip: Units: Pa × m³ = N/m² × m³ = N·m = J.

similar.q: A thermodynamic process in which the temperature of a system remains constant is  A) isobaric.  B) isothermal.  C) isochoric.  D) adiabatic.  E) isometric.
similar.a: B. isothermal. — Isothermal = constant temperature; isobaric = constant pressure; isochoric/isometric = constant volume; adiabatic = no heat exchange (G10 p.96–98). Answer: B.

questions.q: Why desert nights bite?
questions.answer: Dry air + sand low c + clear sky radiates heat away.
why: Dry air + sand low c + clear sky radiates heat away.
questions.label: 20. Why desert nights bite?

similar.q: Q = mcΔθ is used when the temperature changes. What should you use during melting?  A) Q=mL instead  B) Q=0 always  C) Ohm’s law  D) 1/f=1/v+1/u
similar.a: A. Q=mL instead

questions.q: Q = mcΔθ is used when the temperature changes. What should you use during melting?
questions.answer: A
why: Melting is a change of state, and the temperature stays constant.
Q = mcΔθ would give Q = 0 since Δθ = 0 – wrong.
Use latent heat Q = mL – answer A.
questions.tip: Temperature flat on a heating graph → use Q = mL.

similar.q: 2 kg water, c=4200, rise 10 °C. Q?
similar.a: Q=mcΔθ=84000 J.

units.intro: **Temperature** is a quantitative measure of the average kinetic energy of the atoms or molecules in a substance, while **heat** is the spontaneous transfer of thermal energy between systems due to a temperature gradient.
